analysis.investment_thesis: GPIL scores adequately on ROIC (~23% ROCE) but falls short on earnings yield (~6% EBIT/EV), meaning the Magic Formula only half-fires. At 27.6x trailing P/E in a cyclical steel business with earnings already off peak by 40%, the price does not offer a sufficient margin of safety.
key_strengths: Near-zero leverage (D/E: 0.04, borrowings dropped from INR 1,697 Cr in FY20 to INR 192 Cr in FY25) — rare for Indian steel
Vertical integration (iron ore mining → pellets → sponge iron → wire rods) compresses input costs and underpins 23.2% ROCE
Consistent OCF generation (5/5 positive years; OCF averaged ~INR 1,040 Cr FY21-FY24) with strong FCF conversion in non-capex years
key_risks: Steel is a commodity cycle — EBITDA swung from INR 761 Cr (FY20) to INR 1,952 Cr (FY22) and back to INR 1,265 Cr (FY25); ROIC is not durable
Rising capex cycle (INR 538 Cr FY25, CWIP at INR 652 Cr) compressed FCF to just INR 361 Cr — lowest in 5 years, capex/EBITDA now ~43%
Earnings yield barely ~6% (EBIT INR 1,194 Cr / EV ~INR 19,806 Cr) — Magic Formula requires >12% for a genuine bargain; this stock is priced for a recovery
red_flags: Peak earnings distortion: FY22 net profit was INR 1,467 Cr (steel supercycle); trailing P/E of 27.6x is based on normalized, post-peak earnings — makes valuation look deceptively expensive
FCF declining structurally: INR 929 Cr (FY21) → INR 361 Cr (FY25) as capex absorbs cash; capex intensity undermines Magic Formula's preference for asset-light compounders
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on GPIL: EBIT (FY25) = INR 1,194 Cr; EV = Market Cap (INR 19,826 Cr) + Net Debt (INR 309 Cr - INR 329 Cr cash) ≈ INR 19,806 Cr. Earnings Yield = 6.03% — right at my lower acceptable boundary, nowhere near the 12-15%+ I want. ROCE of 23.2% clears the 20% hurdle, but for a cyclical commodity producer this figure oscillates wildly (implied ROCE in FY22 supercycle was dramatically higher; FY20 was sub-15%). A Magic Formula pick needs BOTH metrics firing simultaneously, and here only one does — and marginally at that.

The business itself has genuinely improved: debt nearly eliminated, vertical integration intact, promoter holding steady at 63.5%. But the stock reflects much of this optimism already. Forward P/E of 14.2x implies a significant earnings recovery, which requires steel prices and volumes to cooperate — a bet on commodity timing, not business quality. With FCF shrinking to INR 361 Cr and a new capex cycle underway (CWIP INR 652 Cr), capital allocation is moving toward reinvestment rather than shareholder returns. A steel company with adequate (not exceptional) earnings yield is a HOLD at best until the price falls to push earnings yield above 10%.
